UnrealIRCd UnrealIRCd contains an improper neutralization of delimiters vulnerability that allows any user on a network with two or more linked servers to inject server-to-server commands that are executed with server authority.

Check Point Firewall, Multi-Domain Security Management Server, Scalable Platforms, Security Gateway, and Security Management Server contain an incorrect permissions assignment for critical resources vulnerability when the Gaia OS DynamicCLI daemon runs as root and listens on a world-writable local socket without authenticating connecting processes. An authenticated local user can send a command to the socket and have it executed as root.
Microsoft Office Outlook contains a missing user interaction for potentially unsafe action vulnerability that allows an unauthorized attacker to perform spoofing over a network.

Openwave Messaging Limited Webtop Media Transcoder contains an incorrect resource transfer between spheres vulnerability that may allow an authenticated user to process and convert unintended document types if bypassing the Webmail experience.

Cisco BroadWorks contains an improper restriction of XML external entity reference vulnerability that could allow an unauthenticated, remote attacker to read sensitive configuration information on an affected system.

Barracuda Networks Email Security Gateway (ESG), Load Balancer, Application Delivery Controller (ADC), Message Archiver (BMA), WAF Control Center (WCC), Web Application Firewall (WAF), and Web Security Gateway (WSG) contain an OS command injection vulnerability. This vulnerability could allow an authenticated administrator to inject OS commands that execute with root privileges when the crafted timezone value is subsequently processed. This vulnerability can be chained with CVE-2026-116606

Barracuda Networks Email Security Gateway (ESG) contains an authentication bypass using an alternate path or channel that could allow an unauthenticated remote attacker to invoke a configuration-import function and restore a crafted, compatible backup archive, resulting in unauthorized modification of the appliance’s global configuration. This vulnerability can be chained with CVE-2026-111560.

Google Chromium contains a use-after-free vulnerability in the XML component that could allow a remote attacker to execute arbitrary code inside the sandbox via a specially crafted webpage. This vulnerability could affect multiple web browsers that utilize Chromium, including, but not limited to, Google Chrome, Microsoft Edge, and Opera.

GPUStack contains an improper authentication vulnerability which could allow unauthenticated administrative access, including user and model changes, persistent administrator API-key creation, disclosure of worker and cloud-provider secrets, and code execution through POST /v2/inference-backends/from-yaml.
OpenBSD OpenSSH on Linux contains an unexpected status code or return value vulnerability that could allow for authentication bypass.
SignalWire FreeSwitch contains a code injection vulnerability that permits configuration and credential disclosure, arbitrary call control, and command execution.
IBM Aspera Faspex contains an incorrect authorization vulnerability that could allow an authenticated user to craft a specific message to bypass authorization, causing privilege escalations.

SonicWall SonicOS SSLVPN contains a use of single-factor authentication vulnerability that may allow a user with valid credentials for an alternate authentication method to bypass SAML authentication controls. Successful exploitation may also bypass SAML-enforced multi-factor authentication (MFA).

Apple iOS, iPadOS, macOS, Safari, tvOS and watchOS 10.5 contain an improper authentication vulnerability which could allow an attacker with arbitrary read and write capability to bypass pointer authentication.

WordPress WordPress Core contains a time-of-check time-of-use (TOCTOU) race condition vulnerability that could allow unauthenticated attackers to execute code on the server during the upgrade window. This is due to predictable, web-accessible staging paths used during full-package core upgrades.

Ivanti Connect Secure contains a generation of predictable numbers or identifiers vulnerability that allows a remote authenticated attacker to upload files with attacker-controlled content to a known location on disk. This vulnerability can be chained with CVE-2026-104935 and CVE-2026-111357.

Ivanti Connect Secure contains a missing authentication for critical function vulnerability that could allow a local authenticated attacker to escalate their privileges. This vulnerability can be chained with CVE-2026-104935 and CVE-2026-118527.

GitLab Community Edition and Enterprise Edition contain a integer overflow or wraparound vulnerability that could allow an unauthenticated user to execute arbitrary code on the GitLab server via a specially crafted regular expression in a CI/CD configuration, due to insufficient regular expression validation.

Cisco Secure Firewall ASA Software and Cisco Secure FTD Software contains an unchecked return value to NULL pointer dereference vulnerability that could allow an unauthenticated, remote attacker to cause the device to reload unexpectedly, resulting in a denial of service (DoS) condition.
Broadcom VMWare ESX contains an insufficient logging vulnerability that could allow a malicious actor with admin access to perform certain operations without being logged.

Linux Kernel contains a missing initialization of a variable vulnerability that could allow for unintended modification of page-cache-backed data via failure to preserve the shared-fragment marker during socket buffer coalescing, causing ESP input processing to decrypt shared fragments in place. This vulnerability can be chained with CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 to implant PHP webshells and run commands as root.

Adobe Commerce and Magento contain an unrestricted upload of file with dangerous type vulnerability that could result in arbitrary code execution in the context of the current user, potentially gaining elevated access or control over the victim's account or session.

Google Brotli contains an unchecked return value vulnerability that allows a remote unauthenticated attacker to corrupt adjacent decoder state memory, disclose sensitive memory contents, cause a denial of service, or potentially execute arbitrary code using a crafted Brotli-compressed stream.
PHP contains an out-of-memory corruption vulnerability that allows for unauthenticated remote code execution.
PHP contains a stale internal request-state vulnerability that allows for unauthenticated remote code execution.

Arista VeloCloud Orchestrator on-prem contains a SQL injection vulnerability that may allow a remote attacker to access privileged internal functionality and impact the VCO host. Successful exploitation may compromise the confidentiality, integrity, and availability of the orchestrator and data managed by the orchestrator.

Collabora Collabora Online – Built-in CODE Server when used within the NextCloud platform contains an OS command injection vulnerability that allows for remote code execution when the CODE server isn't running.

EG Secure Solutions SiteGuard Server Edition contains an OS command injection vulnerability which may allow an attacker to execute arbitrary OS commands with root or SYSTEM privileges on the system running the affected product.

Plex Media Server contains an external control of file name or path vulnerability which can allow an admin user to write arbitrary files that may be executed on load. This vulnerability can be chained with CVE-2026-96652, CVE-2026-96654, and CVE-2026-96655.

Plex Media Server contains a server-side request forgery (SSRF) vulnerability that could allow an authenticated user to request arbitrary internal or external addresses via the '/video/:/transcode/universal' path parameter. This vulnerability can be chained with CVE-2026-96652, CVE-2026-96654, and CVE-2026-96656.

Plex Media Server contains an improper neutralization of encoded URI schemes in a web page vulnerability that could allow an attacker to call other plugins' functions and supply their own parameters. This vulnerability can be chained with CVE-2026-96652, CVE-2026-96655, and CVE-2026-96656.

Plex Media Server contains a server-side request forgery (SSRF) vulnerability which could allow an attacker using any X-Plex-Token value to include a full URL in the 'protocol' parameter and force the Plex server to POST to the attacker's chosen destination. This vulnerability can be chained with CVE-2026-96654, CVE-2026-96655, and CVE-2026-96656.

Siemens Software Center contains an uncontrolled search path element vulnerability that could allow an authenticated local attacker to place a specially crafted DLL in a directory that the application searches, leading to arbitrary code execution with the privileges of the affected application.
BeyondTrust Remote Support contains an authentication bypass by spoofing vulnerability that could allow a remote attacker to perform file operations on the appliance.

FortiOS, FortiPAM, FortiProxy, and FortiSwitchManager contain a path traversal vulnerability that may allow an authenticated attacker with admin profile and at least read-write permissions to write or delete arbitrary files via specific CLI commands.

Multiple Atlassian products (Bitbucket Data Center ,Confluence Data Center, Jira Service Management Data Center, Jira Software Data Center, Bamboo Data Center, Crowd Data Center, Crucible and Fisheye) contain a files or directories accessible to external parties vulnerability which could allow an unauthenticated attacker to access specific files within the web application root directory in affected versions.
Memory overflow in Packet Processing can lead to unpredictable or erroneous behavior or Denial of Service in NetScaler ADC and NetScaler Gateway.

Hono is a Web application framework that provides support for any JavaScript runtime. Prior to 4.13.16, csrf() limits origin validation to the content types normally sent by HTML forms and therefore does not validate text/ping requests generated by Chromium hyperlink auditing. Chrome and Edge can send a cross-origin credentialed POST without a CORS preflight through an <a ping> action, and the middleware then skips both Origin and Sec-Fetch-Site checks. The fixed request body limits exploitation to state-changing endpoints whose effect is selected by the path or query string and does not depend on submitted body data. The user's cookie must accompany the request, which generally requires a same-site origin or a cookie configured with SameSite=None, and Firefox does not send hyperlink-auditing pings by default. This issue is fixed in version 4.13.16.

Hono is a Web application framework that provides support for any JavaScript runtime. From 4.5.1 until 4.13.16, validator('form') uses a strict whole-header pattern that fails to recognize multipart/form-data when its Content-Type includes another legal parameter or extra whitespace after a semicolon. The validation callback receives an empty object even though c.req.parseBody() or c.req.formData() can still parse and expose all submitted fields to the handler. An unauthenticated client can therefore bypass allow-list or required-field checks when the application relies on the form validator and its callback accepts an empty object. application/x-www-form-urlencoded requests are not affected. This issue is fixed in version 4.13.16.

Hono is a Web application framework that provides support for any JavaScript runtime. Prior to 4.13.16, mount() and app.mount() can remove a dynamic mount prefix using the route-pattern length rather than the matched-prefix length, allowing a crafted path to be forwarded as a protected inner route while the outer application routes the original path. Since 4.12.21, rebuilding the forwarded URL from the decoded pathname can also convert a decoded backslash to a slash and collapse parent-directory segments, again causing the mounted application to receive a protected path. An unauthenticated client can use either applicable path transformation to reach a mounted route without authentication or authorization middleware scoped to a subpath inside the mount prefix. This issue is fixed in version 4.13.16.

Hono is a Web application framework that provides support for any JavaScript runtime. From 4.1.4 until 4.13.16, RegExpRouter can omit wildcard middleware in three version-specific cases: since 4.13.0, middleware using the explicit default parameter pattern in /api/:tenant{[^/]+}/admin/* is not applied to a route written as /api/:tenant/admin/:id; since 4.1.4, middleware on /admin/* is not applied to a route registered as /admin* for paths under /admin/; and since 4.4.0, a request path containing an encoded line terminator can reach the not-found handler without wildcard middleware. The default SmartRouter selects RegExpRouter for most applications, and the router's registration-time coverage calculation treated the first two matching pattern pairs as different while its compiled wildcard did not match line terminators in the third case. An unauthenticated client can reach a route handler or the not-found handler without authentication or authorization middleware registered on the wildcard path. TrieRouter, LinearRouter, and PatternRouter apply the middleware in the three described cases. This issue is fixed in version 4.13.16.

Hono is a Web application framework that provides support for any JavaScript runtime. From 3.12.0 until 4.13.16, the css helper in hono/css escapes interpolated string values separately and therefore fails to neutralize a closing style tag when < ends the template text or a preceding value and / begins the next attacker-controlled value. During server-side rendering, the combined output can close the <Style /> element early and cause the remainder of the interpolated value to be interpreted as HTML. Applications that place an untrusted string immediately after < in a css template, including adjacent untrusted interpolations, can expose viewers to attacker-controlled HTML or script and information accessible to that page. Other uses of the css helper are not affected. This issue is fixed in version 4.13.16.

OpenTelemetry Python provides the Python API and SDK for OpenTelemetry. Prior to 1.45.2, TraceContextTextMapPropagator.extract() in opentelemetry-api can perform quadratic-time regular-expression backtracking on a malformed traceparent value containing a trace-context prefix, a long whitespace sequence, and an embedded newline. Exploitation requires an attacker-controlled carrier that preserves embedded newlines and permits a sufficiently large value, because conforming HTTP header values cannot contain embedded newlines. JSON-based carriers, including applicable MCP request metadata integrations, can preserve the required newline depending on the SDK, instrumentation, and message-size limits. Parsing on an asynchronous server's event-loop thread can consume excessive CPU and delay unrelated requests, while the advisory does not establish disclosure, modification, or code execution. This issue is fixed in version 1.45.2.

Astro is a web framework for content-driven websites. Prior to 7.4.5, Astro rendered a string used as a dynamic element name as raw HTML after applying an incomplete character filter. A / in the string could make an HTML parser treat the remainder as attributes, allowing untrusted element-name input to inject event-handler markup. The .astro dynamic-tag renderer, JSX renderer, and MDX renderer were affected, and exploitation required an application to use request-controlled or stored untrusted data as all or part of an element name. This issue is fixed in version 7.4.5.

Astro is a web framework for content-driven websites. From 5.7.3 until 9.1.2, the @astrojs/svelte renderer inserted a named slot into the quoted name attribute of an astro-slot wrapper without HTML escaping. Request-controlled slot names containing a quote could terminate the attribute and inject active HTML. Exploitation required a hydrated Svelte component using a client:* directive and dynamic rendering of the attacker-chosen slot; components that did not render that slot emitted only Astro's escaped fallback content. Both server rendering and client-side hydration used the unsafe slot name. This issue is fixed in version 9.1.2.

Astro is a web framework for content-driven websites. From 0.2.0 until 7.1.2, the @astrojs/solid-js renderer inserted a named slot into the quoted name attribute of an astro-slot wrapper without HTML escaping. A request-controlled slot name containing a quote could terminate the attribute and inject active HTML. Exploitation required a hydrated Solid component using a client:* directive and dynamic access to the attacker-chosen slot property; a component that did not render that slot emitted only escaped fallback content. This issue is fixed in version 7.1.2.

Astro is a web framework for content-driven websites. From 5.14.3 until 7.4.7, Astro's /_image endpoint compared the requested local-image path with the build output directory without preserving case on case-sensitive filesystems. A sibling directory whose path differed from the output directory only by letter case could therefore pass the containment check, allowing an unauthenticated requester to read image files accepted by the image service from outside the output directory. Exploitation required on-demand rendering with the @astrojs/node adapter, a case-sensitive filesystem, and a preexisting case-variant sibling directory; ordinary traversal to unrelated paths was already rejected. This issue is fixed in Astro version 7.4.7.

Astro is a web framework for content-driven websites. Prior to @astrojs/prism 4.1.2, and from @astrojs/markdoc 0.3.0 until 2.1.2, runHighlighterWithAstro() returned code unchanged when Prism had no grammar for the requested language, and callers inserted that result as raw HTML. A code block labeled with an unsupported language could therefore render embedded HTML and script instead of displaying it as text. The Prism component was affected when applications supplied untrusted code with an unsupported or attacker-controlled lang, and the @astrojs/markdoc prism() extension was affected for less-trusted content authors even when Markdoc's ordinary HTML rendering was disabled. This issue is fixed in @astrojs/prism 4.1.2 and @astrojs/markdoc 2.1.2.

MessagePack for Ruby is an implementation of the MessagePack binary serialization format. Prior to 1.8.7, the Java-platform msgpack gem for JRuby allocated arrays and byte buffers directly from attacker-controlled array32, str32, and bin32 declared sizes before confirming that corresponding elements or bytes were available. A short MessagePack header could therefore trigger a very large allocation or sustained heap growth when an application decoded untrusted input through MessagePack.unpack or MessagePack::Unpacker, potentially exhausting the shared JVM heap. map32 and declared counts at or above 2^31 did not use the affected allocation behavior. This issue is fixed in version 1.8.7.

@grpc/grpc-js implements the core functionality of gRPC purely in JavaScript, without a C++ addon. Before 1.13.2, and from 1.14.0 through 1.14.1, the @grpc/grpc-js-xds SafeRegexValueMatcher and PathSafeRegexValueMatcher add start and end anchors without grouping a supplied top-level alternation. An expression intended to match one of several complete values can therefore match a prefix, substring, or suffix. The affected matchers are used for route selection, xDS credential identity matching, and RBAC URL path, principal name, server name, and header rules. An ALLOW policy using an alternation can consequently accept a method, certificate identity, or header value outside the intended set, while a DENY policy becomes broader rather than permissive. This issue is fixed in versions 1.13.2 and 1.14.2.

A memory-safety flaw in the key-management request-building component of the library can lead to an out-of-bounds write on the heap. A fixed-size output buffer is used under an assumption about cryptographic key size that is never validated, so when the library is embedded by a caller that supplies its own cryptographic callback implementation, data larger than the buffer can be written past its end. Exploitation requires the ability to control the embedding application's in-process key-management provider configuration, a high-privilege position. The demonstrated impact is memory corruption resulting in abnormal termination of the client process.

A deserialization type-restriction control in the BSON serialization component can be bypassed because the check used to recognize a class of compiler-generated types relies on an overly permissive heuristic rather than a precise identification. An unauthorized party able to supply BSON content that an application later deserializes into a loosely typed member can cause types outside the intended allow-list to be constructed and populated with unauthorized party-supplied values inside the consuming application. This can lead to unexpected object state and errors in downstream application logic. No elevated privileges beyond the ability to place unauthorized party-influenced content in the deserialization path are required.

A type allow-list bypass in the BSON serialization library of the MongoDB C# Driver allows a type-restriction check to be circumvented when polymorphic data is deserialized into loosely typed members. An unauthorized party who can supply or plant BSON/JSON data that the application later deserializes can cause the application process to instantiate .NET types outside the intended allow-list and populate them with unauthorized party-controlled values. In applications that contain a suitable gadget type, this can lead to arbitrary code execution in the context of the application, with corresponding loss of confidentiality, integrity, and availability. No special privileges beyond the ability to introduce data the application reads are required.

Dokploy before 0.31.1 contains a missing ownership check vulnerability in the readAppMonitoring tRPC procedure that allows authenticated attackers to access container metrics belonging to other organizations by supplying an arbitrary appName. Attackers can query getApplicationStats with any application name, including the fixed "dokploy" control-plane service name, to read CPU, memory, network I/O, and block I/O metrics for containers they do not own on self-hosted multi-tenant instances.

A vulnerability has been found in Linksys EA8100 1.0.3.216940. This affects the function GetWANStatus/GetWANStatus3/IsAdminPasswordDefault of the component JNAP API. The manipulation leads to missing authentication. The attack is possible to be carried out remotely. The exploit has been disclosed to the public and may be used. The vendor was contacted early about this disclosure but did not respond in any way.

A vulnerability was found in Linksys EA8100 1.0.3.216940. This vulnerability affects unknown code of the file /jnap/core/CheckAdminPassword. The manipulation results in improper restriction of excessive authentication attempts. The attack may be performed from remote. The attack requires a high level of complexity. It is stated that the exploitability is difficult. The exploit has been made public and could be used. The vendor was contacted early about this disclosure but did not respond in any way.

A vulnerability was determined in Linksys EA8100 1.0.3.216940. This issue affects the function SetRemoteSetting/SetUnsecuredWiFiWarning of the file ui_server.lua of the component JNAP API. This manipulation of the argument isEnabled/enabled causes missing authentication. It is possible to initiate the attack remotely. The exploit has been publicly disclosed and may be utilized. The vendor was contacted early about this disclosure but did not respond in any way.

@grpc/grpc-js implements the core functionality of gRPC purely in JavaScript, without a C++ addon. From 1.14.0 through 1.14.1, XdsServer in @grpc/grpc-js-xds can acknowledge Route and VirtualHost resources while failing to apply their RBACPerRoute override configurations. The override parser is not registered under the override message type, override maps are stored under a type URL instead of the configured HTTP filter name, and VirtualHost override maps are not read. When experimental RBAC is enabled and a trusted xDS control plane supplies a broad top-level ALLOW policy with a stricter matching override, affected servers evaluate RPCs under the broad policy and can accept requests that should be denied. This issue is fixed in version 1.14.2.

Pillow is a Python imaging library. From 1.0 through 12.3.0, ImageFileDirectory_v2.load() in src/PIL/TiffImagePlugin.py retains a separate bytes object for each out-of-line IFD tag value without limiting the total data read or preventing distinct tags from referencing the same file region. A small crafted TIFF or EXIF-bearing JPEG, PNG, WebP, or MPO can therefore cause memory use quadratic in the input size. TIFF and some JPEG paths trigger parsing during Image.open(), while other formats are exposed when EXIF is requested, including through getexif() or ImageOps.exif_transpose(). The declared pixel dimensions do not bound this metadata allocation, so decompression-bomb checks do not prevent process memory exhaustion. This issue is fixed in version 13.0.0.

Pillow is a Python imaging library. From 2.3.0 through 12.3.0, Pillow applications that save compressed TIFF images through libtiff can pass attacker-controlled image geometry tags to the encoder while allocating its row buffer from the actual image dimensions. The affected TiffImagePlugin._save path allows ImageWidth, ImageLength, or SamplesPerPixel from exif=, tiffinfo=, or a source TIFF IFD to make libtiff consume a larger scanline than the buffer supplied by ImagingLibTiffEncode. This can read heap memory into the generated TIFF or crash the process. When TIFF Predictor 2 is enabled, libtiff can rewrite the oversized scanline in place and corrupt memory beyond the buffer. A carried-over PlanarConfiguration value of 2 instead makes libtiff use a shorter scanline and can produce an undecodable output file, but is not established to cause the out-of-bounds access. This issue is fixed in version 13.0.0.

HashiCorp Vault and Vault Enterprise are vulnerable to an issue in the integrated storage join process that may allow an unauthenticated attacker with network access to a new, uninitialized node to cause that node to send credentials from its server environment to an attacker-controlled server. This vulnerability (CVE-2026-92735) is fixed in Vault Community Edition 2.2.2 and Vault Enterprise 2.2.2, 1.21.14, and 1.19.25.

Vault's audit devices did not validate the contents of a configured audit log prefix and did not consistently enforce the server-level setting that restricts audit log prefixing. This may allow a privileged operator to inject content into audit logs, potentially leading to forged or misleading audit records. This vulnerability (CVE-2026-93333) is fixed in Vault Community Edition 2.2.2 and Vault Enterprise 2.2.2, 1.21.14, and 1.19.25.

Vault Community Edition and Vault Enterprise did not consistently apply explicit ACL policy deny rules to request paths that differ only by a trailing slash. This may allow an authenticated user who holds a broader delete permission on system configuration paths to disable a secrets engine, auth method, or audit device that a more specific deny rule was intended to protect. This vulnerability (CVE-2026-93335) is fixed in Vault Community Edition 2.2.2 and Vault Enterprise 2.2.2, 1.21.14, and 1.19.25.

The MCUboot TLV iterator bootutil_tlv_iter_next() in boot/bootutil/src/tlv.c walks image trailer TLVs with a single loop guard (it->tlv_off < it->tlv_end) and advances by sizeof(struct image_tlv) + tlv.it_len using the attacker-controlled it_len field, without validating that the entry's header or payload stays within it->tlv_end. As a result the 4-byte header read can extend up to 3 bytes past the declared TLV area, and the returned (off, len) can describe a payload that runs past it.

The path is pre-authentication: TLVs are parsed during bootutil_img_validate() before the signature is verified, and a crafted image can be presented through DFU / serial-recovery / OTA. However the impact is contained by surrounding guards: bootutil_img_validate() first rejects a TLV area larger than bootutil_max_image_size(), the default LOAD_IMAGE_DATA sink is flash_area_read() which bounds-checks against the flash partition and fails an out-of-partition read, and every payload consumer (EXPECTED_HASH_TLV, EXPECTED_KEY_TLV, EXPECTED_SIG_TLV, IMAGE_TLV_SEC_CNT) clamps len against a fixed buffer before copying.

The residual effect in a default flash build is therefore an out-of-region read confined to the attacker's own slot partition whose result is never observable, yielding at worst a clean validation failure rather than memory corruption or information disclosure. A genuine (though still bounded) out-of-bounds read remains under the non-default MCUBOOT_RAM_LOAD configuration, where LOAD_IMAGE_DATA is an unchecked memcpy. The fix is to validate each entry's header and payload against it->tlv_end inside the iterator.

bootutil_img_hash() computes the image digest over ih_hdr_size + ih_img_size + ih_protect_tlv_size bytes, all three taken from the candidate image's header, and reads that span out of the slot without checking that it fits in the flash area. The three sizes are also summed without an overflow check. Nothing earlier on the validation path bounds the whole span either: bootutil_img_validate() compares the image size against bootutil_max_image_size() only after the hash has been computed.

The callers bound part of the span, or none of it:

On the swap and overwrite upgrade path, boot_validate_slot() first runs the image header check (boot_is_header_valid(), later boot_check_header_valid()). Before MCUboot 2.2.0 that check covered only ih_hdr_size + ih_img_size, so for every image the protected-TLV area (ih_protect_tlv_size, a uint16_t, up to 65535 bytes) was hashed without being bounded. From 2.2.0 the check includes ih_protect_tlv_size, except for a compressed image in the secondary slot when MCUBOOT_DECOMPRESS_IMAGES (CONFIG_BOOT_DECOMPRESSION) is enabled, which leaves the same gap of up to 64 KB.
Zephyr's single-slot and firmware loaders (boot/zephyr/single_loader.c, boot/zephyr/firmware_loader.c) read the header with boot_image_load_header(), which bounds ih_hdr_size + ih_img_size against the flash area. Before MCUboot 2.4.0 that bound did not include ih_protect_tlv_size, which leaves the same gap of up to 64 KB. From 2.4.0 these loaders bound the whole span.
The serial recovery image-list and image-state handlers (bs_list() and bs_set() in boot/boot_serial/src/boot_serial.c) call bootutil_img_validate() with no header check at all, so on those paths ih_img_size is unbounded as well.

The image is hashed before its signature is checked, so anyone who can place an image in a slot (an OTA or SMP update delivered through the application, or serial recovery) reaches this read before authentication.

Whether a malformed header produces an actual read beyond the area depends on the flash backend:

Backends whose flash_area_read() bounds-checks the request (Zephyr, Espressif, NuttX, Mbed) return an error once the chunked read crosses the end of the area. Validation fails and the image is rejected, with no over-read.
With MCUBOOT_HASH_STORAGE_DIRECTLY (Zephyr CONFIG_BOOT_IMG_HASH_DIRECTLY_ON_STORAGE, available from 2.2.0, not enabled by default) the span is hashed through a single direct pointer into memory-mapped flash, with no bounds check.
The Cypress PSoC6 port's flash_area_read() (boot/cypress/cy_flash_pal/cy_flash_map.c, from 1.6.0) does not bound the read: its assert()s compare against the area's absolute offset rather than its size, and it copies with memcpy().

The bytes read past the area feed only the digest, which is compared internally and never returned, so nothing is disclosed. The realistic effect is a read fault during image validation: up to 64 KB past the slot on the upgrade path and, before 2.4.0, on the Zephyr loaders, and potentially much further on the serial recovery handlers, which skip the header check. Where validation is repeated at every boot (a pending upgrade, or, before 2.4.0, the single-slot loader checking its image), the fault can recur on each reset and keep the device from booting.

The fix makes bootutil_img_hash() add the three sizes with boot_u32_safe_add() and reject an image whose span, including the sector offset used in swap-using-offset mode, does not fit in the flash area, before any of it is hashed. Because the bound is applied where the bytes are read, it covers every caller.

In MCUboot's serial-recovery encrypted-image support (boot/boot_serial/src/boot_serial_encryption.c), decrypt_image_inplace() and boot_image_validate_encrypted() each keep a stack-local struct boot_status. boot_enc_load() writes the plaintext per-image AES key into its enckey[] field. Neither function cleared this structure before returning. In addition, a decrypt failure inside the per-sector loop of decrypt_image_inplace() returned early and skipped the total_out: cleanup, which left the expanded AES key context (enc_data) on the stack as well. The error paths of boot_image_validate_encrypted() similarly skipped boot_enc_zeroize().

The affected code is built when encrypted images (MCUBOOT_ENC_IMAGES, Zephyr CONFIG_BOOT_ENCRYPT_IMAGE) are combined with serial recovery. It runs when an encrypted image is uploaded to the primary slot over the recovery protocol, and when the image list or state is queried while an encrypted image is in the secondary slot. After these functions return, the image's AES content key remains in dead stack memory. An attacker who can later read device RAM, for example through a debug port or retained RAM, can recover it.

This weakens the confidentiality of image-encryption keys within the bootloader trust boundary. A recovered key exposes the plaintext of the encrypted firmware image it protects. The device's long-term private decryption key is not exposed. No remote or recovery-protocol channel that returns this memory is known, so exploitation requires a separate memory-read capability.

When MCUboot is built with the TinyCrypt crypto backend (MCUBOOT_USE_TINYCRYPT), bootutil_aes_ctr_drop() in boot/bootutil/include/bootutil/crypto/aes_ctr_tinycrypt.h was an empty stub. The AES-CTR context for this backend is the fully expanded AES-128 key schedule (struct tc_aes_key_sched_struct). Generic code relies on this hook to release and clear key state, so with TinyCrypt nothing was cleared. The mbedTLS and PSA backends do free or destroy their key state here.

As a result, boot_state_clear(), which boot_go() calls before handing off to the application, left the image's AES content-encryption key schedule in the static boot_data state. This is the case after an encrypted upgrade in single-image builds, where boot_enc_zeroize() is not called. boot_decrypt_key() likewise left the ECIES-derived key-encryption key schedule on the stack. The affected build uses MCUBOOT_ENC_IMAGES with TinyCrypt, which is the default ECDSA and Ed25519 backend in the Zephyr port.

The first AES-128 round key equals the cipher key, so anyone who can read the leftover bootloader RAM after boot can recover the image content key and decrypt that encrypted image. That includes a physical attacker with debug or RAM access, or code later running on the device. This weakens image-encryption key confidentiality (and so the confidentiality of the encrypted image's plaintext). The device's long-term private decryption key is not exposed, and image authenticity is not affected. The fix wipes the context with bootutil_wipe_memory().

MCUboot's serial-recovery image-upload handler bs_upload() in boot/boot_serial/src/boot_serial.c declares const struct flash_area *fap = NULL and assigns it only via flash_area_open() part-way through the function. Two early validation failures (goto out_invalid_data) — a CBOR map that fails to decode, or an upload packet missing the off/data members — branch past the open while fap is still NULL, then fall into the shared epilogue. In MCUBOOT_ENC_IMAGES builds that epilogue unconditionally calls boot_handle_enc_fw(fap), which reaches boot_image_load_header() and flash_area_read() and dereferences the NULL flash_area.

The defect is reachable pre-authentication: the trigger is the very first serial-recovery upload command carrying a malformed payload. The guarding conditions are default-true on a fresh recovery session — img_num, curr_off and img_size are zero-initialized statics, so curr_off == img_size and the primary-slot test both hold. It requires a non-default build: encrypted images (MCUBOOT_ENC_IMAGES / Zephyr CONFIG_BOOT_ENCRYPT_IMAGE) together with an active serial-recovery transport, on the Zephyr or Mynewt port (the two that build both boot/boot_serial/src/boot_serial.c and boot_serial_encryption.c with MCUBOOT_ENC_IMAGES).

The impact is a transient denial of service of the bootloader during recovery. fap is a hard NULL rather than an attacker-controlled value, so there is no memory-corruption or information-leak primitive and image authentication is unaffected. Whether the dereference faults is platform-dependent — on targets where address 0x0 is mapped readable flash the read merely returns an error and execution continues, while targets that trap NULL (MPU / null-pointer-exception detection) take a hard fault. Because serial recovery is unauthenticated by design and already permits the console attacker to write the secondary slot, the added capability is only a low-value transient crash.

The related unconditional flash_area_close(fap) call in the same epilogue is a safe no-op on the ports that reach it, so it does not contribute to the dereference.

The affected ports are the Zephyr port — boot/zephyr/CMakeLists.txt compiles boot_serial.c under CONFIG_MCUBOOT_SERIAL and boot_serial_encryption.c under CONFIG_BOOT_ENCRYPT_IMAGE — and the Mynewt port, whose mcuboot_config.h defines MCUBOOT_SERIAL unconditionally and MCUBOOT_ENC_IMAGES under any BOOTUTIL_ENCRYPT_ syscfg, with boot/boot_serial/pkg.yml declaring no explicit source list so the whole directory is built. The Espressif port is not affected**: it compiles boot_serial.c but not boot_serial_encryption.c, and defines no MCUBOOT_ENC_IMAGES, so the #ifdef MCUBOOT_ENC_IMAGES block containing the call is preprocessed away. The NuttX, Cypress and Mbed ports do not build boot_serial.c at all.

boot_save_boot_status() in boot/bootutil/src/boot_record.c reads the image's EXPECTED_HASH_TLV into a stack buffer image_hash[IMAGE_HASH_SIZE] that is never zero-initialised. The TLV handler validates only the upper bound (len > sizeof(image_hash)) and then reads exactly len bytes, so a TLV shorter than IMAGE_HASH_SIZE leaves the tail of image_hash holding stale stack content. The subsequent copy into the boot record, memcpy(buf + offset, image_hash, sizeof(image_hash)), uses the fixed buffer size rather than len, so up to IMAGE_HASH_SIZE - 1 bytes of uninitialised bootloader stack are written into the measured-boot record.

The defect is reachable only under MCUBOOT_MEASURED_BOOT, and only when nothing has checked the length of the hash TLV before boot_save_boot_status() reads it. bootutil_img_validate() rejects a hash TLV whose length is not exactly sizeof(hash) (boot/bootutil/src/image_validate.c:345), and primary-slot validation is on by default (Zephyr's CONFIG_BOOT_VALIDATE_SLOT0 defaults to y), so in a default build the malformed image never reaches this code. Two kinds of build let a short TLV through:

Builds that use pure signatures (MCUBOOT_SIGN_PURE, Zephyr CONFIG_BOOT_SIGNATURE_TYPE_PURE). The signature covers the image itself, so the hash-TLV check in bootutil_img_validate() is compiled out, and a pure-signed image normally carries no hash TLV. A hash TLV is still allowed in the unprotected TLV area, which the signature does not cover, so a short one can be added to a correctly signed image without invalidating it. This applies with every upgrade strategy, including direct-XIP and RAM-load, and the modified image can be delivered through any path that accepts a signed image.
Builds with primary-slot validation turned off: the swap and overwrite loader built without MCUBOOT_VALIDATE_PRIMARY_SLOT, which checks only the image magic before calling boot_add_shared_data(), and the Zephyr single-slot loader (boot/zephyr/single_loader.c) built without it, including the MCUBOOT_VALIDATE_PRIMARY_SLOT_ONCE variant, which skips validation once the trailer records an earlier successful one. Placing the crafted image requires physical or flash-write access to the device; in a single-slot build with serial recovery enabled, the serial-recovery upload writes the primary slot directly and can place it as well. Outside pure-signature builds, the direct-XIP and RAM-load strategies in boot/bootutil/src/loader.c validate the selected slot unconditionally and are not affected.

It is also reachable through a time-of-check/time-of-use change to tamperable external flash between validation and the boot-record read.

In these configurations the boot record's measurement is already not trustworthy: the hash copied into the record is the image's own EXPECTED_HASH_TLV, which nothing has verified and which the attacker chooses. The defect therefore does not weaken attestation integrity any further. What it adds is a path for bootloader memory to leave the device: up to 63 bytes (IMAGE_HASH_SIZE - 1) of uninitialised bootloader stack are embedded in the measurement field that a downstream attestation service sends to a remote verifier. In the configurations analysed the residue is bootloader internal state (TLV offsets and lengths, flash addresses, loop state), not key material, but what occupies that stack region depends on configuration and on which code ran before boot_save_boot_status(). It is reported as a low-severity, defense-in-depth disclosure with no integrity or availability impact.

This is distinct from the already-fixed record_len integer underflow in the same routine (GHSA-8hrv-4cp5-4rg3). The fix rejects any EXPECTED_HASH_TLV whose length is not exactly IMAGE_HASH_SIZE.

MCUboot's Zephyr serial-recovery upload handler bs_upload() in boot/boot_serial/src/boot_serial.c decodes the host-supplied image field of an MCUmgr image-upload request into img_num (a full 32-bit value) and latches it on the off == 0 packet without any range check. It then passes img_num straight to flash_area_id_from_multi_image_slot(img_num, 0), which on the Zephyr port resolves to __flash_area_ids_for_slot() in boot/zephyr/include/sysflash/sysflash.h and indexes the static const int all_slots[] table as all_slots[img_num  2]. That table holds only MCUBOOT_IMAGE_NUMBER  2 entries, so any img_num >= MCUBOOT_IMAGE_NUMBER is an out-of-bounds read.

The path is reachable by anyone with access to the serial / SMP recovery console, which is unauthenticated by design, and the bad value is supplied before any image signature is verified. The defect is specific to the default non-direct upload path (MCUBOOT_SERIAL_DIRECT_IMAGE_UPLOAD disabled) on the Zephyr port with the array-backed slot layout (not CONFIG_SINGLE_APPLICATION_SLOT). It is not gated on a multi-image configuration: MCUBOOT_IMAGE_NUMBER defaults to 1, so even a default single-image build is affected for any image >= 1. The MCUBOOT_SERIAL_DIRECT_IMAGE_UPLOAD path is safe (its flash_area_id_from_direct_image() switch returns -EINVAL for unknown indices).

flash_area_id_from_multi_image_slot() takes a signed int image_index while img_num is uint32_t, so the attacker controls the sign of the index as well as its magnitude: an image of 0xFFFFFFFE converts to -2 and reads all_slots[-4], off the front of the table, while large positive values read off the end (CWE-192). (0xFFFFFFFF itself is the "no image given" sentinel and selects image 0.) Either way the index multiply img * 2 is performed in int, so a wild offset yields a bus/hard fault, giving a reliable denial of service of the bootloader during recovery. For moderately out-of-range indices the read returns adjacent .rodata as a garbage flash-area id that is handed to flash_area_open(); this normally fails with MGMT_ERR_EINVAL, but if the garbage id happens to match a valid non-image partition, the subsequent erase/write can target a partition outside the image set (CWE-787). The attacker-supplied value is never echoed back, so there is no information disclosure. The fix is to reject img_num >= BOOT_IMAGE_NUMBER on the off == 0 packet, before the slot lookup. The comparison must be made on the unsigned img_num: an equivalent guard applied after the conversion to int would not reject the negative case above. __flash_area_ids_for_slot() should bounds-check its own arguments as defence in depth.
This vulnerability was reported independently twice: by NVIDIA Project Vanessa on 2026-06-22, and by Kai Phan (@kaimandalic) on 2026-07-19 as GHSA-8v33-88p6-jffj, which is closed as a duplicate of this advisory. Both original reports are reproduced in full below.

split_image_check() in boot/bootutil/src/loader.c declares a fixed uint8_t loader_hash[32] buffer and passes it as the out_hash out-parameter to bootutil_img_validate(). That routine copies IMAGE_HASH_SIZE bytes into out_hash (memcpy(out_hash, hash, IMAGE_HASH_SIZE) in boot/bootutil/src/image_validate.c), where IMAGE_HASH_SIZE is a compile-time constant of 64 for MCUBOOT_SHA512 or 48 for MCUBOOT_SIGN_EC384/SHA-384 (boot/bootutil/include/bootutil/crypto/sha.h). The buffer tracks SHA-256 (32 bytes) while the copy length tracks the configured algorithm, so the write overruns the buffer by 16 or 32 bytes.

The overflow is only present in a non-default configuration: the legacy Mynewt split-image feature must be compiled (split_go()/split_image_check(), i.e. neither MCUBOOT_DIRECT_XIP nor MCUBOOT_RAM_LOAD), the digest must be larger than 32 bytes (MCUBOOT_SHA512 or MCUBOOT_SIGN_EC384), and MCUBOOT_SIGN_PURE must be off. split_go() is a public API with no caller inside MCUboot; it is invoked from a Mynewt application. In the default SHA-256 build there is no overflow.

The over-written bytes are the one-way digest of the loader image and the overflow length is fixed at build time, so the contents are not meaningfully attacker-controlled and the size is not attacker-chosen. The realistic impact is bounded, uncontrolled corruption of the bootloader's stack on the split-boot path, manifesting as instability or failed boot in the affected configuration rather than reliable code execution. The fix is to size loader_hash to IMAGE_HASH_SIZE and pass IMAGE_HASH_SIZE as the matching seed length.

The MISP Modules website component contains an open redirect vulnerability in its login endpoint. The /login route accepted a user-supplied next query parameter and passed it directly to Flask's redirect() function without validating the destination. An attacker could craft a URL such as https://victim-host/login?next=https://attacker.example/phish and deliver it to a user (e.g., via email or a lookalike page). After the user successfully authenticated, the application issued a 302 redirect to the attacker-controlled external URL. This enables phishing attacks where a user, believing they are still on the legitimate MISP Modules site, may enter additional credentials or sensitive information on the attacker's page. It can also be used to obscure the true destination of a link, bypassing user trust in the legitimate domain. The vulnerability requires the victim to interact with the crafted URL and complete a login, but no prior authentication or special configuration is needed on the attacker's side. The affected component is the website sub-project of misp-modules, specifically the account blueprint in website/app/account/account.py. No version boundaries are specified in the patch metadata.

Edito CMS is vulnerable to improper cryptographic signature verification in the JWT refresh logic. An authenticated low-privilege user can submit self-crafted​ ​JWT​ containing​ ​an existing user​ ​identifier and, due to the lack of signature validation,​​  obtain​ ​a ​​valid,​​ fully-signed​​ session ​​token​​ for​​ any ​​account ​​in​ ​the​ ​system. This allows the attacker to impersonate any user, including administrators.
This issue was fixed in version 5.10.2607.  Hotfixes for older versions (5.8) have also been released.

Edito CMS is vulnerable to Dynamic LINQ injection. Due to improper input validation, an authenticated attacker can inject conditional expressions into the sort parameter of paginated administrative endpoints. Analyzing the returned result order allows the attacker to extract value of any field character by character, leading to potential exposure of sensitive data.


This issue was fixed in version 5.10.2607.  Hotfixes for older versions (5.8) have also been released.

Edito CMS is vulnerable to Stored Cross-Site Scripting (XSS). Due to improper input validation, an authenticated attacker can inject malicious scripts into givenName and surname parameters via the /api/auth/profile endpoint. When an administrator visits the admin changelog logs, the injected script is automatically executed, in his browser.


This issue was fixed in version 5.10.2607.  Hotfixes for older versions (5.8) have also been released.

Edito CMS is vulnerable to Stored XSS via content parameter in Tiny editor functionality. Authenticated attacker can inject arbitrary HTML and JS into website, which will be rendered/executed when user tries to edit changed entry.

This issue was fixed in version 5.10.2607.  Hotfixes for older versions (5.8) have also been released.

Edito CMS is vulnerable to Stored XSS in avatar upload functionality. Authenticated attacker can inject arbitrary HTML and JS into website, which will be rendered/executed when visiting an URL leading to a edited avatar.

This issue was fixed in version 5.10.2607.  Hotfixes for older versions (5.8) have also been released.

Edito CMS restricts the ability to upload files via the UI to specific file types. However, an avatar upload functionality allows an attacker to upload files of any type and extension without restriction.
This issue was fixed in version 5.10.2607.  Hotfixes for older versions (5.8) have also been released.

Edito CMS sends JWT token via GET requests. This allows a local attacker with access to browser history to obtain valid JWT token and perform action on behalf of the victim. The token is valid for only short period of time; after that time, it expires and can no longer be used.



The vendor assessed the likelihood of exploitation as very low and determined that a fix is not necessary.

Edito CMS deserializes JSON data without further validation. A user (even an administrator) cannot exploit this vulnerability through the application's normal functionality. An attacker who could modify cache entries or inject them could execute code on the server.




This issue was fixed in version 5.10.2607.  Hotfixes for older versions (5.8) have also been released.

A flaw was found in Red Hat Quay. The v1 registry API error handler reflects the attacker-supplied image_id path segment in a response served as text/html, allowing a reflected cross-site scripting (XSS) attack. By tricking a user into visiting a specially crafted URL, a remote attacker can execute arbitrary JavaScript in the victim's browser within the Quay origin, potentially compromising the user's session.

OpenMage magento-lts before 20.2.0 contains a stored cross-site scripting vulnerability because the TinyMCE WYSIWYG editor fails to filter scripts in specially crafted HTML tags. Attackers can inject an img element with a malicious onmouseover attribute to execute scripts in the browsers of users viewing the rendered content.

Zipline versions from 3.4.5 before 3.7.10 contain a path traversal vulnerability in the user data export endpoint via the name query parameter. Authenticated attackers can bypass the user id check and use directory traversal sequences to read arbitrary files on the server host.

Zipline through 3.7.9 contains an improper authorization vulnerability in the /api/auth/register endpoint, which enforces invite codes only when user registration is disabled, so registration succeeds without an invite when both invites and user registration are enabled. Unauthenticated attackers can send a direct POST request omitting the invite code to create accounts, view stats, and exhaust storage by uploading many files.

Zipline through 4.3.2 contains a path traversal vulnerability that allows authenticated uploaders to write files outside the upload directory by supplying traversal sequences in the x-zipline-filename header. Attackers using the local datasource can create or overwrite files writable by the Zipline process, corrupting application data or disrupting service.

Zipline before 4.2.1 contains a missing authorization vulnerability in the /api/user/files/transaction endpoint that allows authenticated users to modify other users' files due to absent ownership checks. Attackers who know a target file ID can submit transaction requests to edit or delete files belonging to any user.

Zipline before 4.0.2 contains a predictable filename vulnerability that allows attackers to infer other users' upload filenames by recovering the Math.random generator state. Attackers with five consecutive gfycat-style filenames can reconstruct the random state to predict previous and future filenames until the instance restarts, exposing private uploads.

Zipline before 3.7.12 contains a cross-site scripting vulnerability in the login page that allows attackers to execute JavaScript by supplying an unvalidated url parameter. Attackers can craft a login link with a javascript: URI in the url parameter that executes in the victim's browser after login.

Scapy before 2.7.0 contains an insecure deserialization vulnerability in the load_session function that allows attackers to execute code by supplying a malicious pickle session file. Attackers can trick users into loading a crafted .pkl.gz file via the -s option or conf.session, executing embedded Python code through __reduce__().

An integer overflow vulnerability in the Qt QTextCodec fromUnicode() and toUnicode() functionality of the Qt 5 Core Compatibility APIs module (Qt 6) and the Qt Core module (Qt 5). Only builds where Qt is compiled with ICU support are affected.

Vulnerability due to inadequate restriction of references to external XML entities in OpenKM Community Edition. The XML processing in FormUtils / LocalEntityResolver does not properly restrict the resolution of external resources. An authenticated remote attacker with the ROLE_USER role can exploit the flaw via a REST request. In the 6.3.x branch, this allows the attacker to trigger HTTP requests under their control (SSRF); in 7.0.3, it allows the attacker to read local files and access internal HTTP resources from the server.

The WP STAGING – Backups & Restore, Migration & Clone Plugin – Cloud Backups, Scheduled Backups plugin for WordPress is vulnerable to Arbitrary Directory Deletion in all versions up to, and including, 4.19.0. This is due to insufficient path validation in the `cleanStagingDirectory` function, where the `deleteDir` parameter is only stripped of whitespace and double slashes by `sanitizePath()` without removing `..` traversal sequences or enforcing containment within the staging directory, leaving the sole pre-deletion guard as a simple string equality check against the WordPress home path. This makes it possible for authenticated attackers, with administrator-level access and above, to recursively delete arbitrary directories on the server — including `wp-content`, `wp-admin`, or directories outside the WordPress installation on shared hosting — resulting in denial of service or permanent data loss. An attacker must sequence a clone start, cancellation, and restart to drive the `delete_job` cache into the `directory` step before re-cancelling with a manipulated `deleteDir` value supplied via the `wp_ajax_wpstg_cancel_clone` endpoint.
